# Introduction

In 2014, New York City officials received a Freedom of Information Law request from Chris Whong, who asked for taxi trip data from 2013. Thus, city officials released a dataset containing information about approximately 173 million taxi trips, but not without attempting to anonymize the data first. To protect the privacy of the taxi drivers in the dataset, officials coded the license plate and medallion numbers for each trip before making the information public. However, the predictable nature of license plate and medallion numbers in taxis in New York meant that these coded values were vulnerable to de-anonymization. Vijay Pandurangan proved this in June 2014, when he reversed the anonymization process in less than two hours and was able to link trips back to specific drivers (Goodin, 2014).

This incident only became more controversial when, in October 2014, Northwestern graduate student Anthony Tockar, pointed out that this dataset could reveal information about the passengers in these taxi trips as well (Gawker, 2014). Using the timestamps of paparazzi photos of celebrities entering and exiting taxis, Tockar was able to cross reference the taxi trip dataset to deduce pickup and drop-off locations, the amount of the fare, and make educated guesses regarding how much each celebrity tipped their driver.

This situation highlights several important conversations surrounding data anonymity and the responsibility of organizations when collecting and sharing large amounts of information. While it is important to have public data  to further research and create policy, it is also important to ensure that the ways organizations and government agencies anonymize the data before releasing it are secure.


# Prior Research

## Dan Goodin's Ars Technica Article
The first article I looked at was Dan Goodin's 2014 article, "Poorly Anonymized Logs Reveal NYC Cab Drivers' Detailed Whereabouts," published by Ars Technica. Goodin explains that New York City made over 173 million taxi trip records publicly available after first attempting to protect the privacy of the taxi drivers in these trips. To anonymize the data, the city used a technique called hashing to replace identifiable information like taxi license and medallion numbers with coded values instead. However, Vijay Pandurangan, a software engineer, realized that license plate numbers and medallion numbers are not random strings of digits. Rather, they follow a predictable pattern. By researching this pattern and the MD5 hashing algorithm used to anonymize the data, Pandurangan used computer software to generate possible license and medallion numbers and compare their hashes with the released dataset. Thus, in less than two hours, Pandurangan was able to de-anonymize the entire taxi trip dataset. This meant that individuals could use the in-depth description of all routes taxi cabs took throughout 2013 to potentially identify specific drivers. Additionally, with this location data, it became possible for these individuals to estimate driver earnings, passengers of these trips, and even infer where the drivers lived.

The article also highlights that the use of the MD5 hashing algorithm was not necessarily at fault for the vulnerability of the dataset. Rather, Pandurangan argued that the issue arose from the way the city officials chose to anonymize the information. He noted that officials could have better protected driver privacy by assigning random identification numbers to each driver and taxi, or by using AES encryption with a secret key. These two methods would have made it much harder to reverse the anonymization process and identify the specific drivers. While Pandurangan acknowledged that it would be impossible for New York City officials to have made these changes after releasing the data (since copies of this data had already spread to numerous places), he highlighted that more secure data protection methods needed to be implemented in the future to prevent sensitive information from becoming publicly available.

## Vijay Pandurangan's "On Taxis and Rainbows"

The second article I looked at was an article Vijay Pandurangan wrote on Medium.com titled "On Taxis and Rainbows," which provided more detail into how he was able to de-anonymize such a large dataset. First, the article explains the nuances of the MD5 hashing function. Like all hashing functions, the MD5 algorithm is deterministic, meaning it always produces the exact same hash value for the same input, regardless of how many times the same number is inputted or where it is run. The reason these hash functions are used to anonymize data is because, given the hash value (the output), it is very difficult to determine what the original input is. However, there is an important caveat. If an individual knows something about what the input might look like, the deterministic nature of hash functions makes the anonymized data vulnerable to reverse algorithms, allowing people to uncover the true inputs.

Pandurangan then described the patterns he saw in taxi license plate numbers and medallions. In New York City, taxi license numbers are 6 or 7 digit numbers. Additionally, he realized all 7 digit taxi license plates started with a 5. Thus, Pandurangan was able to conclude that there were only about 3 million possible taxi license numbers. He noted that medallion numbers also followed three specific patterns: one number, one letter, and two numbers, two letters and three numbers, or three letters and three numbers. Thus, Pandurangan found that there are about 19 million possible medallion numbers. With this and the license plate pattern, Pandurangan had 22 million strings of numbers that represented all of the possible inputs the city officials could have provided to the MD5 algorithm. Therefore, by generating the MD5 hashes for all of these numbers and comparing them to the values in the dataset, he was able to reverse the entire anonymization.

Pandurangan explained that generating the hashes took less than two minutes, meaning the entire reversing process took him less than two hours using multiple computers. After explaining how easily the data could be de-anonymized, Pandurangan suggested two alternative methods that could have better protected the taxi drivers' identifiable information. First, he suggested assigning a completely random identification number to each taxi license and medallion number and consistently reusing these numbers throughout the dataset. Implementing this randomization would allow researchers to track the same taxi/driver across multiple trips, meaning the dataset could still be used for research purposes, while also making sure the original license and medallion numbers weren't revealed. More importantly, because these replacement numbers would be random as opposed to based on a predictable pattern, individuals would not be abe to generate a list of possible inputs to match their hashes to the dataset, thus making the MD5 hashing algorithm much more secure. Pandurangan's next suggestion was to create a secret AES encryption key and use the secret key to encrypt each license and medallion number individually. Using secret keys to encrypt data means that individuals would have no way of accessing the original license and medallion data without access to the key itself. Thus, unlike the MD5 hashing algorithm, using keys would make it much more difficult for the drivers' sensitive information to get leaked, and the dataset would still be useful for research purposes (Pandurangan, 2014).


# Ethical Considerations

## Was the data publicly available? Why? How? On What Platform?

An important ethical consideration in data science is whether personal data should be made publicly available, as well as whether the benefits of sharing sensitive data outweigh the potential risks to the individuals represented in the dataset. Making data public allows for researchers, government officials, and other individuals to analyze large amounts of information and thus make more informed decisions, whether that be with regards to policy-making, healthcare, or any other industry. However, organizations also have a responsiblity to consider what information they are releasing and whether doing so could expose individuals to harm.

In the case of this NYC taxi dataset, New York City officials released around 173 million taxi trip records in response to researcher Chris Whong's Freedom of Information Law request. The dataset was given to Chris Whong via a hard drive, who later shared it through downloadable links on his website (Whong, 2014). By granting his request, NYC officials allowed the public to access and analyze lots of sensitive transportation data, which could have helped researchers in a variety of different ways. For example, Whong was interested in the data because he wanted to create data visualizations of how taxis move and operate throughout the city. Additionally, combing through transportation data could allow the city to learn where to implement traffic lights and create more rigid safety measures to ensure pedestrians don't get hurt on busy streets.

However, while the public release of this dataset could have helped researchers studying traffic patterns, the data also contained detailed information about individual trips, including pickup and drop-off locations and timestamps. While officials did attempt to protect the drivers' identities by replacing identifying information with hashed values, they did not consider the possibility that the values could be reversed. Because of this, the dataset's public release created privacy risks for the drivers and the passengers whose trips were recorded. Reversing this anonymization technique meant that many individuals had access to common routes that specific taxi drivers took throughout the year, posing safety threats to these drivers. Ultimately, this taxi incident highlighted that while public access to data can be valuable, government agencies that collect and distribute this information have to ensure that individuals cannot be identified through the data they release, even after direct identifying information has been removed or altered.

## Is the Data Identifiable? Was it Sufficiently Anonymized?

Another important ethical issue in data science is whether personal information is adequately anonymized before it is shared and made publicly available. Anonymization is necessary to protect the individuals in the dataset by removing or changing identifying information, like names, ages, addresses, etc. When anonymization is done right, we have a win-win scenario: the data can be released to the public and remain useful for research, and the identities of the people represented are never revealed. However, perfect anonymization is very difficult to achieve. This is because removing direct identifying information cannot always guarantee anonymity, especially because there are so many other places to obtain information on the internet. Through comparing multiple data sources with the dataset of interest, it is possible to cross reference and thus reconstruct someone's identity.

This is exactly the issue that took place with the NYC taxi dataset. City officials, in an attempt to anonymize the drivers who were taking each taxi route, replaced taxi license and medallion numbers with MD5 hashes. However, because information was available about the way license plates and medallion numbers are constructed for NYC taxis, Vijay Pandurangan was able to generate MD5 hashes for the possible license and medallion numbers and compare them with the hashed values in the released dataset. Thus, in less than two hours, he reversed the anonymization process, linking the trip records back to specific drivers. Additionally, the detailed location and timestamp information in the dataset could be used to infer where drivers lived and even who their passengers were for their trips. For example, in 2014, Anthony Tockar used publicly available paparazzi photographs of celebrities, including Bradley Cooper and Olivia Munn, entering and exiting taxis to match them with records in the dataset and infer their pickup and drop-off locations (Trotter, 2014). 

Through these examples, it is clear that the taxi trip dataset was not sufficiently anonymized. Although not necessarily every individual trip could be linked to a specific person, the dataset contained enough information for people to identify specific drivers and passengers by combining the released dataset with other available information (photos, taxi license patterns, etc). Additionally, the fact that the dataset contained information from 2013 means it was not old enough to be free of privacy concerns when it was released in 2014, especially because this dataset contained detailed information about drivers' daily routines and frequently visited locations.

## Is the data being used in unintended ways to the original study?

A third ethical issue in data science is the possibility that data collected for one purpose might later be used for reasons the individuals in the dataset did not consent to. For example, if data is repurposed in a way that reveals personal information or allows the public to track people's locations, individuals may be exposed to privacy risks they did not consent to. This means that, without proper protection, people can lose control over how their personal information is used.

In this NYC taxi dataset example, the city released millions of taxi transportation records to Chris Whong so he could create visualizations of how taxis moved throughout the city in 2013. When Whong released this supposedly anonymized information to the public, however, individuals quickly found out this dataset could also be used to uncover information about specific drivers and passengers. Pandurangan, for example, showed that the anonymized identifiers could be reversed to identify individual taxi drivers. Anthony Tockar demonstrated that comparing the timestamps of paparazzi photos entering and exiting taxis with the timestamps in the dataset allowed him to infer about their locations throughout the day.

Thus, this taxi trip datset was being used in uninteded ways to the original study. What started out as one individual wanting to create visualizations modeling taxi patterns throughout the city evolved into people pointing out the privacy flaws in the dataset and proving these flaws by tracking passengers using this data and other sources of information on the internet. Ultimately, this situation highlights that while the people that release datasets may do so with good intentions, it is impossible to control all of the ways others might analyze and reuse the information once it becomes publicly available.

## How were the variables collected? Were they accurately recorded? Is there any missing data?

Lastly, it is important to consider whether the variables in a dataset are collected and recorded accurately and whether there is substantial missingness or unreliability in the observations. This quality control matters because researchers and organizations rely on data to make predictions and inform the decisions that affect millions of people. With extensive missingness or inaccurate data collection, the results created by researchers could be misleading.

In the NYC taxi dataset, each row represents an individual taxi trip, and the dataset includes variables like pickup and drop-off times, pickup and drop-off locations, trip distance, fare amount, payment type, and passenger count (NYC Open Data). According to the NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC), these records were submitted by technology service providers who were authorized to collect taxi trip information. Thus, this information was not directly created by TLC itself. Additionally, the different variables were collected in a variety of ways. For example, pickup and drop-off times were recorded when the taxi meter was turned on and off, trip distance was reported by the taximeter, and the number of passengers for each trip was entered by the driver (NYC Open Data). This means that while some of the variables were generated through the taxi's electronic systems, other variables depended on human data entry, which could potentially introduce human error. Additionally, if the taxi's electronic system was malfunctioning, more errors could be introduced into the data collection.

Additionally, there is evidence that the original dataset contained missing/unreliable observations. In a 2015 research paper analyzing this 2013 NYC taxi dataset, researchers Marjan Momtazpour and Naren Ramakrishnan explained that they had to remove several missing values from the data set. For example, they removed trips with invalid geographical coordinates, trips with identical pickup and drop-off locations, and trips with no passengers (Momtazpour & Ramakrishnan, 2015). Additionally, some information wasn't captured in the dataset at all. For example, the TLC's trip record data dictionary notes that the tip amount variable only counts tips paid with a credit card, meaning tips paid with cash are not recorded in the variable (New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission, 2025). This means that a researcher analyzing driver earnings using this dataset could underestimate the actual amount drivers received in tips.

# Conclusion: Why Does This Matter?

This NYC taxi dataset situation highlights that officials that release data need to balance the benefits of making data publicly available with protecting the privacy and safety of the individuals represented in that dataset. As discussed above, making millions of taxi trip records available to the public can benefit researchers and government officials who want to use the information to study traffic activity or make more informed decisions about city planning and/or public safety. However, because the data was not anonymized in a secure way, the travel patterns and (in many cases) the identities of taxi drivers and their passengers could be uncovered by analyzing the dataset with other publicly available sources. This meant that taxi drivers could have their work routines and locations exposed, while passengers could have their private trips inferred all without consent.

In this situation, these ethical concerns were not necessarily driven by profit; however, they are connected to surveillance. In releasing a dataset with detailed information about millions of trips without adequately protecting the information of the taxi drivers (and indirectly, their passengers), NYC gave the public access to information that could be used to monitor the movements of many people. Additionally, individuals whose information was included in the dataset, as mentioned in the ethical considerations, could not control how other people analyzed or reused their information. Ultimately, this incident highlights the fact that while public access to data is important to benefit a society, these benefits cannot come at the expense of the privacy/safety of those in the dataset. Thus, organizations that collect and release this data have an ethical responsibility to consider the downsides that come with making data public alongside the potential values of releasing it.
